meta.title: Complexity: predict before you measure
meta.objective: predict the growth class of a piece of code before you run it
meta.audience: students who have seen loops and arrays but not formal analysis
meta.source: CLRS, Introduction to Algorithms (3rd ed.), ch. 3; Sedgewick & Wayne, Algorithms (4th ed.), §1.4

steps.prompt: Which of these grows slowest as n gets large?
steps.why: The whole point of the notation: it is about the shape of the curve, not the constant.
steps.hint: Compare them at n = 1,000,000. Which one barely notices?

options.feedback: Yes — doubling n adds one step, whatever n is.
Not wrong as a guess, but log n is strictly slower-growing: n doubles when n doubles, log n adds 1.
This is the sorting bound — faster than n², but it still grows faster than n.
This is the fastest-growing option here, not the slowest.

steps.prompt: Put each operation in the bucket its cost grows like.
steps.why: Recognising the shape of a loop is most of the analysis you will ever do.
steps.hint: A single index into an array is one step. A loop over half the array is not.

items.text: binary search of a sorted array
for x in arr: total += x
halving the search range on each pass

steps.prompt: Order these from slowest-growing to fastest-growing.
steps.why: Ranking functions is how you compare two designs without running either.
steps.hint: Constants are invisible here. n log n sits between n and n².

steps.prompt: Binary search on a sorted array of 1024 elements. At most, how many comparisons?
steps.why: Turning log n into a number you can say out loud is the difference between knowing the notation and using it.
steps.feedback: Right: 2¹⁰ = 1024, so ten halvings reach one element. Doubling the array adds exactly one comparison.

steps.prompt: Which of these are O(n log n)? Select all that apply.
steps.why: This is the class most real algorithms live in, and the one students misremember as O(n²).
steps.hint: One of these is n² in the worst case, whatever the average case looks like.

options.feedback: Yes — log n levels, each level merging n elements.
Yes — n extractions from a heap, each costing log n.
Worst-case quicksort is n² — that is exactly why the average case is worth stating separately.
Insertion sort is n² in general, though it is linear on nearly-sorted input.

steps.prompt: What do we call the fact that constants are ignored? (one word)
steps.why: Naming the idea makes it retrievable later.
steps.hint: It starts with 'a' and the notation uses a capital O.
steps.feedback: Asymptotic — the statement is about behaviour as n grows without bound, not about any particular machine.

steps.prompt: In your own words: why does doubling n add only one comparison to binary search?
steps.why: Self-explanation is what turns a remembered fact into a working model.
steps.hint: Think about what each comparison does to the range, not to n.
steps.reveal: Each comparison halves the remaining range. Doubling n means one more halving is needed to get down to a single element — the work grows with how many times you can halve, which is log n. Nothing about the comparison itself gets harder.

steps.prompt: You must choose between an O(n²) loop and an O(n log n) routine. What actually decides it?
steps.why: The misconception this exercise exists to kill: the notation ranks growth, and growth only dominates at scale.
steps.hint: At what n does the difference start to matter, and how large does n actually get?

options.text: The input size the code will actually see, and the constants
options.feedback: Right. Below a few dozen elements the constant dominates and the quadratic version can win; the notation tells you what happens as n grows, not what happens at n = 12.

options.text: The lower asymptotic class always wins
options.feedback: This is the trap. Asymptotics describe growth, not your actual n — and they hide the constants that dominate small inputs.

options.text: Whichever one has fewer lines of code
options.feedback: Readability matters, but it is not the complexity question being asked here.
